blocks.robotComment: Hey, I'm Swipey! 👋 Let's find out what makes C# tick. 🤖
blocks.body:
C# (pronounced "C sharp") is a modern, general-purpose programming language created by Microsoft. It was designed to build all kinds of software — from desktop apps and websites to video games and cloud services.

C# is "object-oriented". This means: you build your program out of small, reusable building blocks called "objects" — for example, an object could be a "player" or a "bank account", each with its own properties (e.g. health, balance) and abilities (e.g. jump, withdraw money).

code.caption: This is a complete, runnable C# program. It simply prints the text "Hello, C#!".

blocks.question: What does this program print when you run it?
options: Nothing — it needs more code first
blocks.explanation: Console.WriteLine(...) prints exactly what's inside the quotes, so this program prints "Hello, C#!".

blocks.sentence: C# is a programming language that is ___, meaning it works with objects.
blocks.explanation: C# is object-oriented — programs are built from objects with properties and abilities, not just a list of commands.

blocks.robotComment: Strongly typed sounds strict, but it catches your mistakes early. 🛡️
blocks.body: C# is also "strongly typed". This means every piece of data has a specific, known kind — such as a whole number or a piece of text — and the language checks that you use it correctly before your program ever runs. This helps catch many mistakes early, instead of letting them cause surprises later.

blocks.robotComment: C# doesn't run alone — it needs a whole platform behind it. 🧩
blocks.body: C# does not work by itself — it is built to run on ".NET" (pronounced "dot net"), a free platform from Microsoft that provides the tools and libraries a C# program needs to actually execute. You will learn much more about how this works later in this level.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Careful — this one is easy to get backwards.
blocks.statement: C# was created by Google.
blocks.explanation: C# was created by Microsoft — not by Google.

blocks.robotComment: Ever wonder why there's a little '#' stuck to the end of 'C'? Let's find out. 🎵
blocks.body: The story of C# begins in the late 1990s at Microsoft. A team led by lead architect Anders Hejlsberg set out to design a new language for building modern software on Windows. The result was first released to the public in 2002, alongside Microsoft's new ".NET Framework".

blocks.question: Who led the design of C# at Microsoft?
blocks.explanation: C# was designed by Anders Hejlsberg and his team at Microsoft.

blocks.robotComment: That little # symbol has a musical secret. 🎼
blocks.body: The name "C#" comes from music notation, where a "sharp" (#) raises a note by a half step — hinting that C# is a step up from the older language C. Visually, the "#" symbol also looks a bit like four "+" signs packed together, a playful nod to C++, another language C# borrowed heavily from.

blocks.sentence: The "#" in C# comes from music notation, where a "___" raises a note by a half step.
blocks.explanation: A "sharp" in music raises a note by a half step, which inspired the name "C#".

blocks.body: C# has kept evolving steadily ever since. C# 3 (2007) introduced LINQ, a powerful way to query data. C# 5 (2012) added async/await for writing responsive, non-blocking code. C# 9 (2020) arrived alongside .NET 5, the release that unified Microsoft's once-separate ".NET Framework" (Windows-only) and ".NET Core" (cross-platform) into a single, modern ".NET" platform.

blocks.robotComment: Open source means anyone can peek under the hood. 🔓
blocks.body: Unlike many older Microsoft technologies, C# and .NET are open source today. Their source code is publicly available on GitHub, and developers all over the world — not just Microsoft employees — contribute improvements to the language.

blocks.statement: C# and .NET are open source, with source code publicly available on GitHub.
blocks.explanation: Both the C# compiler and the .NET platform are open source and hosted publicly on GitHub.

blocks.robotComment: Picking your first language is a big decision — here's why C# is a great one. 🎯
blocks.body: There are many programming languages — so why is it worth learning C# specifically? For one, C# is incredibly versatile: with the .NET platform behind it, the exact same language can build a website, a phone app, a desktop program, and a video game.

blocks.robotComment: Video games are a huge draw for a lot of people learning C#. 🎮
blocks.body: One especially popular reason people learn C#: it is the main scripting language for Unity, one of the most widely used game engines in the world. If you dream of making your own games, C# is often the very first language you'll need.

blocks.question: Which widely used game engine uses C# as its main scripting language?
blocks.explanation: Unity is one of the most popular game engines, and it uses C# for scripting game behavior.

blocks.sentence: C# is the main scripting language used by the ___ game engine.
blocks.explanation: Unity, a leading game engine, uses C# as the language developers write their game logic in.

blocks.robotComment: Strict rules now save you a lot of headaches later. 🛡️
blocks.body: C# also teaches you excellent fundamentals. Because it is strongly typed with very clear rules, you get used to writing organized, predictable code right from the start — habits that transfer well to almost any other language you learn afterward.

blocks.robotComment: Enterprise, cloud, games — C# shows up almost everywhere. 🏢
blocks.body: Finally, C# has a strong job market. It is heavily used in enterprise software, cloud services built on Microsoft Azure, and game studios — meaning solid demand for C# developers across many different industries.

blocks.statement: C# can only be used to build one specific type of application.
blocks.explanation: C# is highly versatile — it is used to build websites, desktop apps, mobile apps, games, and cloud services, not just one type of application.

blocks.robotComment: You'll be surprised how many places run on C#. 🌍
blocks.body: C# and .NET show up in more places than you might expect at first glance. Here are the most important areas where C# is used today.
🎮 Video games: Unity, one of the most popular game engines, uses C# for all gameplay scripting — from small indie games to major mobile and console hits.

blocks.question: Which of these is a well-known use case for C#?
options: Scripting games built with the Unity engine
Styling web pages with colors and fonts
blocks.explanation: C# is the primary scripting language for Unity, making it hugely popular among game developers.

blocks.robotComment: Windows and C# have a long history together. 🖥️
blocks.body: 🖥️ Desktop applications: Many Windows desktop programs are built with C#, using frameworks like WPF (Windows Presentation Foundation) or Windows Forms.

blocks.sentence: Many Windows desktop programs are written in C# using frameworks like ___ or Windows Forms.
blocks.explanation: WPF (Windows Presentation Foundation) and Windows Forms are two popular frameworks for building C# desktop apps.

blocks.body: 🌐 Web backends: Using a framework called ASP.NET Core, many companies build the "server side" of their websites and apps in C# — the part that processes and stores data behind the scenes.

blocks.robotComment: One language, phones, tablets, and desktops all at once. 📱
blocks.body: 📱 Cross-platform apps: With .NET MAUI, developers can write a single C# codebase that runs as a native app on Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS.

blocks.statement: C# is only used for small private hobby scripts.
blocks.explanation: C# is used at a very large scale — from Unity games to enterprise web backends and cross-platform apps, not just small scripts.

blocks.robotComment: Source code is just text you write — the .NET tools turn it into something real. 📝
blocks.body: When you write a C# program, you type text into a file — for example Program.cs. This human-readable text is called "source code". It consists of words and symbols that follow strict, well-defined rules, but is still readable to you.

code.caption: This is source code. You can read and understand it, even if you don't know every detail yet.

blocks.body: A computer, however, cannot execute this text directly. A processor only understands "machine language" — tiny electrical signals represented as zeros and ones. Source code is therefore an intermediate stage: understandable for humans, but not yet directly executable by the hardware.

blocks.robotComment: Think about what a processor actually understands before you answer. 🤔
blocks.statement: A computer processor can execute C# source code directly, without translating it first.
blocks.explanation: A processor only understands machine language. C# source code must first be translated before it can be executed.

blocks.body: C# source code is always saved in files with the extension ".cs". Unlike some other languages, C# does not require the file name to match the name of a class inside it — you could name the file above "Greeting.cs" and it would still work fine, as long as it's part of the project.

blocks.sentence: C# source code files always have the file extension ___.
blocks.explanation: Source code files in C# always end in ".cs" — for example "Program.cs".

blocks.robotComment: You've got the starting point down — next up, how it becomes runnable. ➡️
blocks.body: In summary: source code is the starting point of every C# program. It is the text that you, as a developer, write, read, and edit yourself. Later — with the help of another tool — this text becomes something the computer can actually execute. You will learn about that tool in the next lesson.

blocks.question: What best describes "source code"?
options: The human-readable text that you write in a C# file (.cs)
The zeros and ones that the processor understands directly
A program that installs other programs
A file that only contains images
blocks.explanation: Source code is the human-written and human-readable text of a program, stored in a .cs file.

blocks.robotComment: Your code needs a translator before the computer can run it — meet the compiler. 🔧
blocks.body: You now know that source code is human-readable, but the computer cannot execute it directly. This is exactly where the "compiler" comes in — a program that translates your source code into something closer to what a computer can process.

The C# compiler is called "Roslyn". It reads your .cs file(s) and translates them into a new form that can eventually be run. This process is called "compiling", and today it's most commonly triggered with a single command using the .NET command-line tools.

code.code: dotnet build
code.caption: This is how you typically trigger compilation: the "dotnet" command-line tool calls the C# compiler for you.

blocks.sentence: The modern C# compiler is called ___.
blocks.explanation: "Roslyn" is the name of the compiler platform that compiles C# source code today.

blocks.robotComment: CIL is the next big idea — we dig into it properly next lesson. 👀
blocks.body: Important: the compiler does not translate your code directly into machine language for a specific processor. Instead, it produces a special intermediate form called "Common Intermediate Language", or CIL — more on that in the next lesson. This intermediate form is a big part of what makes .NET so flexible across different platforms.

The compiler also checks your code for errors. If, for example, you made a typo or forgot a bracket, the compiler stops with an error message and does not produce a translated file. This is called a "compile error" (or "build error").

blocks.question: What happens if your C# source code contains a typo?
options: The compiler stops with an error message and does not produce a translated file
The compiler ignores the error and just keeps going
blocks.explanation: If the compiler finds an error in the source code, it reports a compile error and does not produce a runnable translated file.

blocks.robotComment: Think carefully about what the compiler actually produces. 🕵️
blocks.statement: The C# compiler translates source code directly into machine language for a specific processor.
blocks.explanation: The compiler translates source code into Common Intermediate Language (CIL) — a platform-independent intermediate form, not directly into machine language for a specific processor.

blocks.robotComment: Compiling does not produce a finished program yet — there is a step in between. 🔍
blocks.body: When the compiler (Roslyn) translates your source code, the result is not a finished file specifically for Windows, macOS, or Linux — it produces "Common Intermediate Language", or CIL for short. CIL is an intermediate form: no longer human-readable source code, but also not machine language for one specific processor.

CIL is packaged into a file called an "assembly", usually with the extension ".dll" (or ".exe" for a program you run directly). So after compiling, "Program.cs" ends up inside an assembly such as "Program.dll".

code.code:
dotnet build
// produces an assembly containing CIL, e.g. Program.dll
code.caption: The compiler reads your .cs files and produces an assembly full of CIL from them.

blocks.sentence: The C# compiler produces an intermediate form of code called ___.
blocks.explanation: The compiler translates C# source code into Common Intermediate Language (CIL), packaged inside an assembly.

blocks.body: What is special about CIL is that it is platform-independent. This means the very same assembly can be used on a Windows PC, a Mac, or a Linux server — the CIL itself is identical everywhere. No recompiling needed for each operating system!

blocks.statement: CIL is different for each operating system and must be freshly generated for Windows, macOS, and Linux.
blocks.explanation: CIL is platform-independent — the same assembly works on every operating system without being recompiled.

blocks.robotComment: This combo is exactly what makes cross-platform .NET possible. 🌐
blocks.body: CIL still isn't what the processor directly understands, though. It is designed specifically to be read by another program — the Common Language Runtime (CLR), which you will learn about in the next lesson. It is exactly this combination of CIL and the CLR that lets the very same compiled program run on many different operating systems.

blocks.question: Why is CIL so important for C# and .NET?
options: Because it is platform-independent and works on any operating system with a matching CLR
Because it is executed directly by the processor, without further help
Because it is easier for humans to read than source code
Because it completely replaces the .cs file, which can then be deleted
blocks.explanation: CIL is platform-independent — it runs anywhere a CLR is available, without the code needing to be rewritten for every system.

blocks.robotComment: CIL needs someone to actually run it — say hello to the CLR. 👋
blocks.body: You have learned that the compiler produces CIL (packaged inside an assembly) from your source code. But who actually executes this CIL? The answer: the "Common Language Runtime", or CLR for short.

The CLR is a program that runs on your operating system and reads CIL. Using a technique called "Just-In-Time" (JIT) compilation, it translates the CIL into the machine language that your specific device's processor understands — right as the program runs, whether that's a Windows PC, a Mac, or a Linux server.

code.code: dotnet run
code.caption: This is how you start a program on the command line: the "dotnet" tool hands your compiled assembly to the CLR, which JIT-compiles and runs it.

blocks.sentence: The CLR uses ___-In-Time compilation to translate CIL into machine language as the program runs.
blocks.explanation: "Just-In-Time" (JIT) compilation is the technique the CLR uses to translate CIL into machine code right when it's needed.

blocks.robotComment: The CLR does more than just translate — it looks after your program too. 🛡️
blocks.body: Beyond translating CIL, the CLR also manages important background tasks for your program: it automatically frees up memory that is no longer needed (a process called "garbage collection"), enforces C#'s strong typing rules, and handles errors that occur while the program is running.

blocks.statement: The CLR automatically manages memory for a running C# program through garbage collection.
blocks.explanation: The CLR includes an automatic garbage collector that frees memory your program no longer needs.

blocks.robotComment: Watch how these three pieces line up into one complete pipeline. 🔗
blocks.body: The complete process looks like this: you write Program.cs (source code). The Roslyn compiler translates it into an assembly containing CIL. The CLR reads that assembly and executes it, JIT-compiling the CIL into machine code for your device along the way.

blocks.question: What is the main job of the Common Language Runtime (CLR)?
options: It executes CIL, translating it into machine code and managing memory while the program runs
It writes source code automatically for you
It stores C# files in the cloud
blocks.explanation: The CLR runs the compiled CIL, JIT-compiling it to machine code and handling tasks like memory management.

blocks.robotComment: Time to find out where the compiler and the CLR actually come from. 📦
blocks.body: You now know three building blocks: source code, the compiler (Roslyn), and the CLR. But where do you actually get these tools? The answer: you install the ".NET SDK" (Software Development Kit).

The .NET SDK is a complete package for developers. It contains everything you need to write, build, and run C# programs: the compiler, the CLR, a large collection of ready-made libraries, and the "dotnet" command-line tool that ties it all together.

code.code:
dotnet build   // Part of the SDK: compiles source code into an assembly
dotnet run     // Part of the SDK: builds and then runs the program
code.caption: Both of these commands rely on tools bundled inside the .NET SDK.

blocks.sentence: Anyone who wants to write and compile C# programs installs the ___.
blocks.explanation: The .NET SDK contains the compiler and all the tools needed to write and build C# programs.

blocks.robotComment: Think of it like a full workshop — everything you need is already inside. 🧰
blocks.body: You can think of the .NET SDK like a complete workshop: it contains not just the machine that runs the finished product (the CLR), but also all the tools needed to actually produce that product in the first place (the compiler and more).

blocks.robotComment: Not everyone needs the full toolbox, though. 🎬
blocks.body: If you only want to run a finished .NET program without developing your own, a smaller ".NET Runtime" install (which includes just the CLR) is enough. Developers, however, need the full .NET SDK, since it includes the runtime plus the compiler and everything else needed to actually build software.

blocks.question: What is included in the .NET SDK?
options: The compiler, the CLR, libraries, and the dotnet command-line tool
Only a text editor for writing notes
Only the CLR, but no compiler
Only a collection of icons and logos
blocks.explanation: The .NET SDK bundles the compiler, the CLR, libraries, and the dotnet CLI — everything developers need to build C# programs.

blocks.statement: You can check whether the .NET SDK is installed correctly by running "dotnet --version".
blocks.explanation: Running "dotnet --version" prints the installed SDK version, confirming your setup is working.

questions.sentence: Human-readable C# text is stored in a file with the extension ___.
questions.explanation: C# source code files always use the ".cs" extension.

questions.statement: A processor can execute C# source code directly, without translating it.
questions.explanation: A processor only understands machine language — source code must be translated first.

questions.question: What is the modern C# compiler called?
questions.explanation: Roslyn is the compiler platform that compiles C# source code today.

questions.statement: If the compiler finds an error in the source code, it still produces a runnable file.
questions.explanation: When the compiler finds an error, it reports a compile error and does not produce a runnable file.

questions.sentence: The compiler translates source code into ___, packaged inside an assembly.
questions.explanation: The compiler produces CIL, an intermediate, platform-independent form of the code.

questions.statement: CIL is platform-independent and works with any matching CLR.
questions.explanation: The same CIL assembly can run on Windows, macOS, or Linux, as long as a matching CLR is available.

questions.question: What does the Common Language Runtime (CLR) do?
options: It executes CIL by translating it into machine language for the respective device
It stores .cs files in the cloud
questions.explanation: The CLR executes compiled CIL, using Just-In-Time compilation to translate it into machine code.

questions.sentence: Developers install the ___ in order to write, compile, and run C# programs.
questions.explanation: The .NET SDK includes the compiler, the CLR, and other tools developers need to build C# programs.

questions.question: What technique does the CLR use to translate CIL into machine code as a program runs?
questions.explanation: The CLR uses Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation to translate CIL into machine code while the program runs.

questions.statement: The order of the C# pipeline is: write source code, translate it into CIL with the compiler, execute it with the CLR.
questions.explanation: This is exactly the pipeline: source code (.cs) becomes CIL via the compiler, then the CLR runs the CIL.

blocks.robotComment: Every C# program needs a home for its code — that's exactly what a class gives it. 🏠
blocks.body: In C#, the code you write typically lives inside a class. A class is like a container or blueprint that holds your program's code together — its data and the actions it can perform.

code.caption: The keyword "class" followed by the name of the class — here the class is called "Program".

blocks.robotComment: Notice how 'public' opens the door for other code to use this class. 🚪
blocks.body: The keyword "class" tells the C# compiler: "A new class starts here." Sometimes it is preceded by "public" — this means the class is visible and usable from other parts of a larger project, not just within its own file.

code.caption: This is also a valid (still empty) class — it's simply called "Car" instead of "Program".

blocks.sentence: In C#, the code you write typically belongs inside a ___.
blocks.explanation: C# code typically lives inside a class. Methods are part of the code too, but they themselves are located inside a class.

blocks.robotComment: Capital letters for class names — small rule, big consistency win. 🔤
blocks.body: By convention, a class name starts with a capital letter and uses "PascalCase" for multiple words — for example "Program", "Car", or "BankAccount". This isn't a strict compiler rule, but practically every C# developer follows it so code looks consistent for everyone.

blocks.question: What best describes a class in C#?
options: A container or blueprint that holds your code together
A single number in the program
A comment that the compiler ignores
An error message from the compiler
blocks.explanation: A class is the container that holds C# code — comparable to a blueprint that ties everything together.

blocks.robotComment: Every C# program needs at least one of these to get anywhere. 🏗️
blocks.body: For everything you'll learn in this level, a C# program's code is housed inside at least one class. Next, we'll look at how a program inside such a class actually starts running: with the Main() method.

blocks.statement: A class name conventionally starts with a lowercase letter in C#.
blocks.explanation: By convention, C# class names start with a capital letter (PascalCase), such as "Program" or "Car".

blocks.robotComment: Every C# program needs exactly one starting line — this is it. 🚀
blocks.body: Every C# program needs a starting point — a place where execution begins. This starting point is a very specific method called Main(). When you start a C# program, the Common Language Runtime (CLR) automatically looks for this method.

code.caption: As soon as you start this program, the CLR finds the Main() method and begins execution right there.

blocks.robotComment: This is a fun one to get right — capitalization matters here! 🔠
blocks.body: The line "static void Main()" is called the method's signature. "static" means the method belongs to the class itself (you don't need an object to start it), and "void" means the method doesn't return a value. Note the capital "M" in "Main" — this is different from languages where the entry point is lowercase, so it's an easy detail to trip over.

blocks.question: What does the CLR look for to start a C# program?
options: A method called Main() with the exact signature
The first line in the source code, regardless of what it says
The longest method in the entire program
blocks.explanation: The CLR specifically looks for a method called Main() — with a capital M — as the starting point of the program.

blocks.robotComment: Even one wrong letter here and things will not start as expected. ⚠️
blocks.body: If the method name isn't exactly right — for example "main" with a lowercase "m" — it will not be recognized as the program's entry point. Capitalization matters everywhere in C#, and the Main() method is a perfect example of why.

blocks.sentence: For a C# program to start, the CLR looks for a method called ___ (with a capital first letter).
blocks.explanation: C# names its program entry point "Main" — with a capital "M" — unlike some other languages that use a lowercase name.

blocks.robotComment: Next up: what exactly counts as a 'statement' in C#. ➡️
blocks.body: Inside the Main() method, you write your program's actual statements — they are executed step by step, in the order they appear. We'll take a closer look at exactly what a "statement" is in the next lesson. (You may also spot a newer, shorter style called "top-level statements" in modern C# code, which skips writing the class and Main() by hand for small programs — but understanding the classic form first makes that shortcut much easier to understand later.)

blocks.statement: In C#, the program's entry point method must be named exactly "Main", with a capital M.
blocks.explanation: The CLR only recognizes "Main" — capitalized — as the entry point of a C# program.

blocks.robotComment: A semicolon is C#'s way of saying 'done with this thought.' ✅
blocks.body: A C# program consists of many small statements. A statement is a single instruction to the computer — for example "print this text". Every statement ends with a semicolon ";".

code.code: Console.WriteLine("Hello, C#!");
code.caption: This is a single statement. It ends with a semicolon — the character that tells C# "done".

blocks.robotComment: Forget this tiny character and the compiler gets confused fast. ⚠️
blocks.body: The semicolon works like a period at the end of a sentence: it tells the compiler "this statement is complete, the next one follows". If you forget the semicolon, the compiler doesn't understand where a statement ends and reports an error.

code.caption: Here are two statements in a row. C# executes the first one first, then the second — in exactly that order.

blocks.statement: Every statement in C# must end with a semicolon.
blocks.explanation: A semicolon marks the end of every single statement in C#. Without this character, the compiler doesn't understand where the statement ends.

blocks.robotComment: No shortcuts yet — C# just runs your code top to bottom. ➡️
blocks.body: At its core, a C# program is nothing more than a sequence of such statements. The CLR processes them strictly in order — from top to bottom, one after another. At this point there are no "shortcuts" or jumps yet — it's purely step-by-step execution.

blocks.question: Which character marks the end of a statement in C#?
blocks.explanation: A semicolon (;) marks the end of every statement in C#.

blocks.body: Statements don't just float around freely — they always sit inside a block enclosed by curly braces { }, for example the block of the Main() method. We'll see exactly how these blocks work in the next lesson.

blocks.sentence: C# executes a program's statements in order, from ___ to bottom.
blocks.explanation: C# processes statements strictly in the order they appear in the code — from top to bottom.

blocks.robotComment: Curly braces are how C# knows where a group of code starts and ends. 🧱
blocks.body: Curly braces { } group multiple statements together into a shared block in C#. A block marks a clear beginning and a clear end — for example the body of a class or the body of a method.

code.caption: The outer curly braces belong to the class "Program", the inner ones to the Main() method.

blocks.robotComment: See how one block can live neatly inside another. 📦
blocks.body: Blocks can be nested inside one another, similar to a box inside another box. The block of the Main() method lies completely inside the block of the class — it starts later and ends earlier than the class block.

code.caption: Marked with comments, you can clearly see: the method block lies entirely within the class block.

blocks.question: What are curly braces { } used for in C#?
options: To group related statements into a block
blocks.explanation: Curly braces { } group statements into a block, for example the body of a class or a method.

blocks.robotComment: Miss a closing brace and the compiler will let you know. ⚠️
blocks.body: Every opening brace { must eventually have a matching closing brace }. If one is missing, the compiler can't tell where a block ends and reports an error — even if the rest of the code is correct.

blocks.statement: Every opening curly brace { needs a matching closing brace }.
blocks.explanation: In C#, braces must always come in pairs. If a closing brace is missing, the code can't be compiled.

blocks.body: As a reminder: the class itself is a block, the Main() method is another block inside it, and the individual statements from the last lesson sit inside these blocks. That's how everything in a C# program fits together.

blocks.sentence: The block of the Main() method lies ___ the block of the class.
blocks.explanation: The method block is nested inside the class block — it lies completely within it.

blocks.robotComment: Time to pull together everything you have learned about the rules. 📋
blocks.body: You now know about classes, the Main() method, statements, and code blocks. Let's summarize a few basic syntax rules that apply to every C# program.

code.code:
Console.WriteLine("Hello!"); // correct
console.writeline("Hello!"); // Error! C# is case-sensitive
code.caption: C# is "case-sensitive" — capitalization makes a difference. "Console" and "console" are two completely different words as far as C# is concerned.

blocks.robotComment: Case matters everywhere in C# — no exceptions. 🔠
blocks.body: This applies to everything in C#: class names, method names, keywords like "class" or "static". A single letter with the wrong capitalization leads to a compiler error.

Unlike some other languages, C# does not require the file name to match the name of a class inside it — a file can be named anything ending in ".cs". Even so, most C# developers name their file after the main class it contains, purely as a helpful convention.

code.caption: This code would compile just fine whether it lives in "Program.cs", "Main.cs", or any other ".cs" file name.

blocks.statement: C# is case-sensitive (for example, "Main" and "main" are different).
blocks.explanation: C# is case-sensitive: capitalization matters everywhere, including class names and method names.

blocks.body: Indentation — meaning spaces at the start of a line that visually shift nested blocks inward — is, on the other hand, not necessary for the compiler. C# compiles code without any indentation just fine. Still, you should always indent cleanly, because it makes your code much easier for people to read.

code.caption: This code compiles just fine — it's simply much harder to read without indentation than the indented version above.

blocks.question: Which statement about indentation in C# is correct?
options: It is not necessary for the compiler, but it makes the code more readable
The compiler requires exactly four spaces of indentation
Without indentation, the code won't compile
Indentation replaces the semicolon at the end of a statement
blocks.explanation: Indentation only serves human readability. The C# compiler doesn't require it — semicolons and curly braces are the actual rules.

blocks.robotComment: You now have the complete rulebook for any C# program. 📖
blocks.body: In summary, every C# program follows these rules: the code lives in a class, execution starts in the Main() method, every statement ends with a semicolon, related statements sit in a block of curly braces, and C# is case-sensitive throughout.

blocks.sentence: In C#, a file containing your code must end with the extension ___.
blocks.explanation: Every C# source file ends in ".cs", regardless of what the file is named otherwise.

questions.question: What best describes a class in C#?
options: A container or blueprint that holds your code together
A single number in the program
A comment that the compiler ignores
An error message from the compiler
questions.explanation: A class is the container that holds C# code together, like a blueprint.

questions.statement: A class name conventionally starts with a lowercase letter in C#.
questions.explanation: By convention, C# class names start with a capital letter (PascalCase).

questions.sentence: A C# program begins its execution in the ___ method.
questions.explanation: C# names its entry point "Main", with a capital M.

questions.question: Which keyword in the Main() signature means the method doesn't return a value?
questions.explanation: "void" means the method doesn't return a value after it runs.

questions.statement: A statement in C# must always end with a semicolon.
questions.explanation: Every statement in C# ends with a semicolon (;).

questions.sentence: C# executes a program's statements ___ (from top to bottom).
questions.explanation: C# processes statements strictly in the order they appear, from top to bottom.

questions.sentence: Curly braces { } group statements into a ___.
questions.explanation: Curly braces group related statements together into a block.

questions.statement: Every opening curly brace { needs a matching closing brace }.
questions.explanation: Braces always come in pairs in C#. A missing closing brace causes a compiler error.

questions.question: Does the name of a C# file have to match the name of a class inside it?
options: No, C# does not require this, though it is a common convention
Yes, it is a strict compiler rule
Only if the class is public
questions.explanation: Unlike some other languages, C# does not require the file name to match a class name — it is just a common convention.

questions.statement: C# is case-sensitive.
questions.explanation: Capitalization matters everywhere in C#, from keywords to class and method names.

blocks.robotComment: Time to make C# actually say something out loud. 🔊
blocks.body: To display text on the screen (the "console") in C#, you use the command Console.WriteLine(). It outputs whatever text you pass to it in parentheses and double quotation marks.

code.caption: This complete program outputs exactly one line: Hello, World!

blocks.robotComment: That "Line" at the end is doing more work than you would guess. 📏
blocks.body: The word "Line" in WriteLine tells you exactly what happens after the output: the cursor automatically moves down to a new line. So the next piece of output begins below it, not right after it.

code.caption: Two WriteLine() calls produce two separate lines.

blocks.sentence: Console.WriteLine() outputs text and then automatically moves to a new ___.
blocks.explanation: WriteLine always finishes by moving the cursor down one line, so the next output starts fresh below it.

blocks.body: Console is a class that lives in the System namespace, which is why your file starts with "using System;" — that line tells the compiler where to find Console. WriteLine is the name of the method you are calling on it. The text in parentheses and double quotes is a "string" — exactly what gets printed to the screen.

code.caption: Without "using System;", you would have to write out System.Console.WriteLine() in full every time, as the first line shows.

blocks.question: What happens right after Console.WriteLine("Hi"); outputs its text?
options: The cursor automatically moves to a new line
The next output is appended directly after it, with no line break
blocks.explanation: WriteLine() always inserts a line break after the output — the next output starts on a fresh line.

blocks.robotComment: Miss the quotation marks here and the compiler gets very confused. ⚠️
blocks.body: Important: the text you want WriteLine() to output must sit inside double quotation marks, for example "Hello". Without them, the compiler would try to interpret the text as program code — like a variable or keyword — rather than as plain text, and your program would fail to compile.

blocks.statement: Console.WriteLine() outputs text without any line break, exactly like Console.Write().
blocks.explanation: That is not true: WriteLine() always adds a line break after the output. Write(), which you will meet next, does not — that is exactly what tells the two commands apart.

blocks.robotComment: Write() is WriteLine()'s more low-key sibling — no automatic new line. 🔇
blocks.body: Besides Console.WriteLine(), there is also Console.Write(). It works almost the same way, but with one important difference: Write() does NOT move to a new line afterward.

code.caption: Both pieces of text end up right next to each other on the same line — no space and no line break in between.

blocks.robotComment: The cursor just... stays put. That is the whole trick. 📍
blocks.body: That is the key difference from WriteLine(): after Write(), the cursor stays exactly where the text ends, and the next output is appended directly after it.

code.caption: "A" is printed with no line break, so "B" lands right next to it. WriteLine() then breaks the line, so "C" starts fresh below.

blocks.question: What does this code output?
options: "XY" on one line, then "Z" on a new line
"X" on one line, then "Y" and "Z" together on the next line
"X", "Y", and "Z" each on three separate lines
blocks.explanation: Write("X") leaves no line break, so "Y" is appended directly: "XY". WriteLine("Y") then breaks the line, so "Z" begins on a new one.

blocks.body: Write() is handy when you want to build a single line of output from several separate calls. Just remember: you have to add any spaces yourself — Write() never adds one for you.

code.caption: The spaces are deliberately placed at the end of "C# " and "is " — otherwise the words would run together.

blocks.sentence: Console.Write() outputs text but does not add a ___ afterward.
blocks.explanation: That is exactly the difference from WriteLine(): Write() outputs the text but leaves the cursor on the same line.

blocks.statement: After Console.Write("Hi"); the next output automatically begins on a new line.
blocks.explanation: False — Write() does not produce a line break. The next output lands right after "Hi", on the same line.

blocks.question: What is the main difference between Console.Write() and Console.WriteLine()?
options: WriteLine() moves to a new line after the output, Write() does not
Write() cannot output numbers, but WriteLine() can
WriteLine() is only meant for debugging programs
There is no difference — both behave identically
blocks.explanation: WriteLine() always adds a line break at the end, while Write() leaves the cursor on the same line. That is the only difference, but it matters a lot.

blocks.robotComment: Some characters need a little help to show up in your text. 🔡
blocks.body: Sometimes you want to output something that cannot simply be typed as-is — for example a line break in the middle of a sentence, or a quotation mark. For this, C# has "escape characters": a backslash (\) followed by a letter that carries a special meaning.

code.caption: \n produces a line break — in the middle of a single WriteLine() call.

blocks.sentence: The escape character ___ produces a line break in the middle of a piece of text.
blocks.explanation: \n stands for "newline" and produces a line break, even though it sits inside a single WriteLine() call.

blocks.body: The escape character \t produces a tab — a larger, even amount of spacing. This lets you roughly line up text into columns.

code.caption: \t makes "Max" and "17" line up roughly underneath each other, even though "Name:" and "Age:" have different lengths.

blocks.question: What is the escape character \t used for?
blocks.explanation: \t inserts a tab, a larger, even amount of spacing that helps align text into columns.

blocks.robotComment: This trick lets a quotation mark exist peacefully inside a string. 💬
blocks.body: If you try to place a regular quotation mark in the middle of a piece of text, there is a problem: C# would think the string ends right there. The fix is \" — an "escaped" quotation mark that is treated as plain text instead of the end of the string.

code.caption: Without the backslashes before the inner quotation marks, the compiler would end the string too early and report an error.

blocks.robotComment: Even backslashes need their own special trick to print. ⚙️
blocks.body: And what if you actually want to output a backslash itself — for example in a file path? Since a single backslash normally starts an escape character, you have to double it: \\.

code.caption: Each \\ in the code produces exactly one real backslash in the output.

blocks.statement: To output a single backslash, you must write \\ in the code rather than just \.
blocks.explanation: A lone backslash is treated as the start of an escape sequence, so C# requires you to double it (\\) to print one real backslash.

blocks.robotComment: One little dollar sign unlocks a much cleaner way to build text. 💲
blocks.body: C# has a very convenient feature called "string interpolation". By placing a $ symbol right before the opening quotation mark, you can drop curly braces { } directly into your text, and whatever is inside them gets calculated and inserted into the output automatically.

code.caption: The expression inside { } is evaluated first, and the result is inserted right into the text.

blocks.body: You are not limited to math — you can put almost any expression inside the curly braces, and C# will convert the result to text for you automatically. Soon, once you learn about variables, you will use interpolation constantly to weave their values straight into your output.

code.caption: Each pair of curly braces is replaced with the result of the expression inside it.

blocks.sentence: To create an interpolated string in C#, you place a ___ symbol directly before the opening quotation mark.
blocks.explanation: The $ prefix turns a normal string into an interpolated one, activating the { } placeholders.

blocks.robotComment: Curly braces are special here, so escaping them takes a little extra typing. 🔧
blocks.body: Because { and } now have a special meaning inside an interpolated string, you need to double them (using {{ and }}) if you actually want to print a literal curly brace.

code.caption: The doubled {{ }} around "Score" print as literal braces, while the single { } around 100 is evaluated as an expression.

blocks.question: What does this line output?

code.code: Console.WriteLine($"Total: {10 + 5}");

options: An error, because interpolation is invalid here
blocks.explanation: The expression 10 + 5 inside the curly braces is evaluated first, so the output shows the result, 15.

blocks.statement: An interpolated string in C# must start with a $ symbol before the opening quotation mark.
blocks.explanation: Without the leading $, curly braces would just be printed as plain text characters instead of being evaluated.

blocks.robotComment: This one habit will replace a lot of clunky concatenation later on. 🧵
blocks.body: String interpolation is usually the cleanest way to combine fixed text with calculated values, and most C# developers reach for it by default instead of gluing pieces of text together by hand.

questions.question: What happens automatically after Console.WriteLine("Hi"); outputs its text?
options: The cursor moves to a new line
questions.explanation: WriteLine() always inserts a line break after the output.

questions.statement: Console.Write() automatically adds a line break at the end, just like Console.WriteLine().
questions.explanation: Write() does not add a line break — that is exactly what separates it from WriteLine().

questions.sentence: The escape character ___ produces a line break in the middle of a piece of text.
questions.explanation: \n stands for "newline" and inserts a line break wherever it appears.

questions.question: What does this code output?

code.code:
Console.Write("A ");
Console.WriteLine("test");

questions.explanation: Write() leaves no line break, so "test" is appended right after "A " on the same line.

questions.statement: \t produces a tab that helps align text into columns.
questions.explanation: \t inserts a tab, a larger, even amount of spacing.

questions.sentence: To output a quotation mark directly inside a string, you write ___.
questions.explanation: An escaped quotation mark, \", is treated as plain text instead of ending the string.

questions.question: Why do you have to write \\ to output a single backslash?
options: Because a single backslash starts an escape sequence in C#
Because C# does not allow backslashes at all
Because a single backslash ends the program
questions.explanation: A lone backslash begins an escape sequence, so it must be doubled to print a literal one.

questions.sentence: To create an interpolated string, you place a ___ symbol directly before the opening quotation mark.
questions.explanation: The $ prefix activates the { } placeholders inside an interpolated string.

questions.question: What does Console.WriteLine($"Total: {10 + 5}"); output?
questions.explanation: The expression inside the curly braces is evaluated first, so the result 15 is inserted.

questions.statement: To print a literal curly brace inside an interpolated string, you write it as {{ or }}.
questions.explanation: Doubled braces {{ }} print as literal braces, since single braces are reserved for expressions.

blocks.robotComment: Comments won't run, but they might just save future-you a headache. 📝
blocks.body: A comment is a note in the code that the C# compiler completely ignores. Comments never change what a program does — they exist purely for humans who read the code: yourself a few weeks from now, or teammates who look at it later.

code.caption: The compiler skips the line with the comment entirely — it has no effect whatsoever on the program.

blocks.statement: Comments are executed by the C# compiler like normal code.
blocks.explanation: Comments are completely ignored by the compiler. They have no effect whatsoever on what the program does.

blocks.robotComment: A comment that just repeats the code isn't pulling its weight. 📝
blocks.body: Code you write today, you often don't look at again until weeks or months later — and by then you may have forgotten why you wrote certain lines the way you did. A good comment immediately explains what's going on, without forcing you to re-read and re-think the entire block of code.

code.code:
// TODO: Add an evening greeting later
Console.WriteLine("Good morning!");
code.caption: A TODO comment is a reminder to yourself or your team about work that still needs to happen.

blocks.sentence: A comment that marks an open task for later often begins with the word ___.
blocks.explanation: TODO comments are a widely used convention for marking open tasks directly inside the code.

blocks.robotComment: This WHY vs WHAT distinction is the whole secret to good comments. 💡
blocks.body: Comments are especially valuable when they explain WHY something is done in the code — not just WHAT is done. The "what" can usually be read straight from the code itself. The "why", on the other hand, only exists in the mind of whoever wrote it.

code.caption: This comment explains the intent behind the code — information you couldn't guess from the code alone.

blocks.question: What are comments in C# mainly intended for?
options: For humans who need to read and understand the code
For the compiler, to avoid errors
To make the program run faster
blocks.explanation: Comments are aimed at humans. The compiler ignores them completely — they make the program neither faster nor slower.

blocks.robotComment: Two slashes and you're commenting — C#'s simplest kind of note. ✏️
blocks.body: The simplest way to write a comment in C# is with two forward slashes: //. Everything on the same line after // is completely ignored by the compiler.

code.caption: The line with // is ignored. The Console.WriteLine line runs completely normally.

blocks.body: A single-line comment does not have to sit on its own line. It can also appear directly after code on the same line — this is called an "inline comment."

code.code: Console.WriteLine("Hello!"); // prints "Hello!" to the screen
code.caption: C# runs the code before the // and simply ignores everything after it on that line.

blocks.sentence: A single-line comment in C# begins with the characters ___.
blocks.explanation: Two forward slashes (//) start a single-line comment in C#.

blocks.robotComment: Turning off code without deleting it is a handy trick. 🔌
blocks.body: With //, you can also temporarily "turn off" a line of code without deleting it. This is called "commenting out." C# then treats the line as if it were not there at all.

code.caption: "Line 2" is never printed because that line is commented out. Only "Line 1" and "Line 3" appear.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
blocks.explanation: The middle line is commented out and therefore skipped. Only "A" and "C" are printed.

blocks.robotComment: One small catch about how far a // comment actually reaches. 👀
blocks.body: Important: // only comments out text up to the end of the current line. A line break automatically ends the comment — the next line is read as normal code again.

blocks.statement: A // comment automatically also applies to the next line of code.
blocks.explanation: A // comment automatically ends at the end of the line. The next line is treated as normal code again.

blocks.robotComment: Sometimes one line just is not enough room to explain yourself. 📄
blocks.body: Sometimes a single line isn't enough to explain something. For longer notes, C# has a second notation: the multi-line comment. It begins with /* and ends with */ — everything in between is ignored, no matter how many lines it spans.

code.caption: Everything between /* and */ is ignored by the compiler — even across multiple lines.

blocks.robotComment: This style is perfect for describing a whole file right at the top. 🗂️
blocks.body: Multi-line comments are especially well-suited for longer explanations — for example, describing at the top of a file what a program actually does.

code.caption: The asterisks (*) at the start of each line are just a visual convention many developers follow. For the compiler, all that matters is that everything sits between /* and */.

blocks.sentence: A multi-line comment in C# begins with /* and ends with ___.
blocks.explanation: A multi-line comment is opened with /* and must be closed again with */.

blocks.body: Another practical use: with /* */ you can "turn off" several lines of code at once, without having to add // in front of every single one.

code.caption: Both "Middle" lines are completely skipped — only "Start" and "End" are printed.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
blocks.explanation: The block between /* and */ is completely ignored. Only "Start" and "End" are actually printed.

blocks.robotComment: Forgetting to close this one causes a very confusing kind of bug. ⚠️
blocks.body: An important difference from //: a multi-line comment always has to be closed with */. If you forget it, the compiler treats all the following code up to the next */ as one giant comment — which can lead to very confusing errors.

blocks.statement: A multi-line comment /* ... */ can span multiple lines.
blocks.explanation: That is exactly the advantage of /* */ over //: the comment can span any number of lines until it is closed with */.

blocks.robotComment: You know the syntax — now for writing GOOD comments. ✍️
blocks.body: You now know both kinds of comments in C#: // and /* */. But just as important as the syntax is knowing when and how to use comments effectively. Here are the most important rules for good comments.

Rule 1: Explain the WHY, not the WHAT. Good code is often already self-explanatory — what it does is visible from the code itself. A comment is usually only helpful when it explains the reasoning behind a decision.

code.caption: Both comments sit above the same line of code — but only the second one adds information the code alone doesn't show.

blocks.statement: The comment "// prints Hello" above Console.WriteLine("Hello"); is an example of a good comment.
blocks.explanation: The comment merely repeats what the code already shows clearly. A good comment would instead explain why this line exists.

blocks.robotComment: A comment that lies is worse than no comment at all. ⚠️
blocks.body: Rule 2: Keep comments up to date. When the code changes but the comment doesn't, you end up with an outdated comment — which is often worse than no comment at all, because it misleads whoever reads it next (including future you).

code.code:
// Prints the user's first name
Console.WriteLine("Welcome back!");
code.caption: This comment was probably not updated after the code changed — it no longer describes what the line actually does.

blocks.sentence: A comment that no longer matches the current code is called ___.
blocks.explanation: A comment that no longer matches the changed code is outdated — and can actively mislead.

blocks.robotComment: Comment overload can actually make code harder to read. 🌀
blocks.body: Rule 3: Don't over-comment. If every single, obvious line gets its own comment, the code becomes cluttered instead of clearer. Use comments purposefully — to mark sections or explain genuinely tricky parts. As a bonus, C# also has a special triple-slash comment (///) used to generate reference documentation for your code, which you will encounter later once you start writing your own methods.

code.caption: Comments should appear where they truly provide guidance — not on every simple line.

blocks.question: When is a comment most useful?
options: When it explains why something is done, or usefully marks a section
When it appears before every single line of code
When it simply repeats what the code already shows
When it is as long as possible
blocks.explanation: Comments are most valuable when they add context or reasons that aren't obvious from the code itself — not when they merely repeat it.

questions.question: What are comments in C# mainly used for?
options: To make code more understandable for humans
To make the program run faster
questions.explanation: Comments exist purely for humans reading the code — the compiler ignores them completely.

questions.statement: The C# compiler executes the text inside a comment like normal code.
questions.explanation: Comments are completely ignored by the compiler and have no effect on the program.

questions.sentence: A single-line comment in C# begins with the characters ___.
questions.explanation: Two forward slashes (//) start a single-line comment.

questions.question: What happens to the code after // on the same line?
options: It is ignored by the compiler
It is automatically deleted from the file
questions.explanation: A // comment silently ignores everything after it up to the end of that line.

questions.statement: A single-line comment starting with // automatically also applies to the next line.
questions.explanation: A // comment ends at the line break — the next line is read as normal code again.

questions.sentence: A multi-line comment begins with /* and ends with ___.
questions.explanation: A multi-line comment must be explicitly closed with */.

questions.question: What is a multi-line comment (/* ... */) especially well-suited for?
options: Longer explanations, or turning off multiple lines of code at once
questions.explanation: /* */ can span any number of lines, making it ideal for longer notes or disabling a whole block.

questions.statement: With /* */, you can comment out multiple lines of code at once.
questions.explanation: Everything between /* and */ is ignored, no matter how many lines it spans.

questions.question: What makes a comment genuinely useful, according to good commenting practice?
options: It explains why a line of code exists, not just what it does
It repeats exactly what the code already shows
It appears above every single line of code
It is written in the longest possible sentence
questions.explanation: The "what" is usually visible from the code itself — a good comment adds the "why".

questions.statement: An outdated comment that no longer matches the code can do more harm than good.
questions.explanation: A comment that no longer reflects the code can actively mislead whoever reads it next.

blocks.robotComment: Variables are how your program remembers things — let's give data a name. 📦
blocks.body: A variable is a named container that stores a piece of data your program can work with and change while it runs. In C#, every variable must have a declared type, so the compiler always knows exactly what kind of data it is allowed to hold.

code.code:
int age = 25;
Console.WriteLine(age);
code.caption: Declaring an int variable named age, giving it the value 25, and then printing it.

blocks.robotComment: Notice how this pattern reads almost like a sentence: type, name, value. 🔤
blocks.body: The general pattern for declaring and initializing a variable is: type name = value;. Here, int is the type, age is the name, and 25 is the value assigned with the = operator. You don't have to assign a value right away — you can declare a variable first and give it a value later, as long as you assign something before you try to use it.

blocks.robotComment: Naming rules feel picky at first, but they make code predictable. 📛
blocks.body: Variable names in C# must start with a letter or an underscore (_) — never a digit — and cannot be one of C#'s reserved keywords (like class or int). Names are case-sensitive, so score and Score are two different variables. By convention, C# developers write variable names in camelCase: the first word is lowercase, and each following word starts with a capital letter, e.g. totalScore or firstName.

blocks.sentence: In C#, variable names conventionally use ___, where the first word is lowercase and every following word starts with a capital letter, such as totalScore.
blocks.explanation: C#'s naming convention for local variables and method parameters is camelCase — lowercase first word, capitalized following words, no underscores.

blocks.body: A variable can also be reassigned: given a new value after it was already initialized. The new value simply replaces the old one — the old value is gone. The new value must still be compatible with the variable's declared type, since C# is statically typed and never lets a variable suddenly hold a different kind of data.

code.caption: Reassigning a variable using its own current value is a very common pattern, for example when tracking a changing score or a countdown.

blocks.robotComment: This shortcut is everywhere in real C# code — good to recognize early. 👀
blocks.body: C# also offers a shortcut called implicit typing with the var keyword: if you initialize a variable right away, C# can figure out its type on its own, so you can write var instead of spelling out the type. The variable still has a fixed, specific type underneath — var is just a convenience for you as the person typing the code.

code.caption: var can only be used when a value is assigned on the same line, since that value is how the compiler figures out the type.

blocks.robotComment: Quick gut check on how reassignment actually works. 🤔
blocks.statement: Once you declare a variable's type, you must write that type again every time you assign it a new value.
blocks.explanation: You only specify the type once, at declaration. After that, you simply write variableName = newValue; without repeating the type.

blocks.robotComment: A handful of built-in types carry almost all the data in a C# program. 🧮
blocks.body: Every variable in C# needs a type, and the built-in primitive types are the most basic kinds of data a variable can hold. Primitives store a simple value directly, which makes them fast and memory-efficient — unlike the string type you will meet soon, which is a reference type.

code.caption: Four commonly used primitive types: a whole number, a decimal number, a true/false value, and a single character.

blocks.robotComment: Four everyday types, four different jobs. 🔡
blocks.body: int stores whole numbers (no decimal point) and is the default choice for counting things. double stores decimal numbers and is the default choice for anything with a fractional part, like prices or measurements. bool can only ever be true or false, which makes it perfect for yes/no conditions — note that C# spells it bool, not boolean. char stores exactly one character, written in single quotes like 'A' — never double quotes, which are reserved for strings.

blocks.sentence: To store a single character like 'A', you use the ___ type.
blocks.explanation: char stores exactly one character and uses single quotes, unlike string, which uses double quotes and can hold many characters.

blocks.body: C# also has smaller and larger whole-number types for when int isn't the right fit: byte and short save memory for tiny numbers, while long is used for whole numbers bigger than int can hold — you mark a long literal with an L at the end. For money and other values needing exact decimal precision, C# offers decimal, marked with an m suffix; it is more precise than double but slightly slower to calculate with.

code.caption: long needs an L suffix and decimal needs an m suffix on their literal values; byte is useful for very small numbers where saving memory matters.

blocks.robotComment: Local variables don't get the same free pass as fields — keep that in mind here. 🤔
blocks.body: Fields that belong to a class automatically get a default value if you don't initialize them — 0 for numeric types, false for bool, and a null character for char. Local variables declared inside a method, however, do not get a default value: the compiler forces you to assign one before you can use the variable, which helps catch bugs early.

blocks.statement: A local variable declared inside a method automatically gets a default value, like 0, if you never initialize it.
blocks.explanation: Local variables have no default value in C# — the compiler reports an error if you try to use one before assigning it a value.

blocks.question: Which primitive type would you use to store whether a light switch is on or off?
blocks.explanation: bool is designed exactly for two-state, true/false values like on/off.

questions.question: What must every variable in C# have?
questions.explanation: C# is statically typed — every variable needs a type so the compiler knows what it can hold.

questions.statement: In C#, variable names are case-sensitive, so score and Score are different variables.
questions.explanation: C# treats identifiers as case-sensitive, so differently-cased names refer to different variables.

questions.sentence: C#'s naming convention for local variables is ___, e.g. totalScore.
questions.explanation: Local variables and parameters follow camelCase by convention in C#.

questions.question: Which statement correctly declares and initializes an int variable named age?
questions.explanation: The pattern is type name = value; — int age = 25; follows it exactly.

questions.statement: You can declare a variable without giving it a value right away, as long as you assign one before using it.
questions.explanation: A declared but unassigned local variable is fine, as long as it gets a value before it is read.

questions.sentence: The ___ type stores whole numbers and is the most common choice for counting things.
questions.explanation: int is the default whole-number type in C#, used for counting and everyday integer values.

questions.question: Which type would you use to store a value like 4.99?
questions.explanation: double is the default type for numbers with a fractional part.

questions.statement: A local variable inside a method automatically receives a default value if you don't initialize it.
questions.explanation: Unlike class fields, local variables get no default value — the compiler requires you to assign one first.

questions.sentence: A long literal in C# must end with the letter ___.
questions.explanation: An L suffix marks a numeric literal as a long instead of the default int.

questions.question: What happens when you reassign a variable that already holds a value?
options: The old value is replaced by the new one
questions.explanation: Reassignment simply overwrites the previous value with the new one.

blocks.robotComment: Strings look simple, but under the hood they work differently from int. 🧵
blocks.body: string is one of the most-used types in C#, but it works differently from the primitives you just learned: string is a reference type, not a primitive. A string variable doesn't store the text directly the way an int stores a number — it stores a reference to a string object living elsewhere in memory. In everyday code, though, you can create and use strings almost as easily as primitives.

code.caption: The + operator concatenates (joins) strings together, while $"..." lets you interpolate values directly into the text.

blocks.robotComment: No parentheses needed for this one — it is a property, not a method. 📏
blocks.body: string comes with many useful members. Length is a property (not a method — no parentheses!) that tells you how many characters are in the string. You can also grab a single character at a given position, counting from 0, using square brackets right after the variable name.

code.caption: word.Length has no parentheses, since it is a property. word[0] is the character at index 0.

blocks.sentence: To find out how many characters are in a string, you read its ___ property.
blocks.explanation: Length is a property on string (accessed without parentheses) that reports the number of characters it contains.

blocks.body: The Substring(start, length) method returns a new string containing a chunk of the original: it begins at the given start position and includes exactly length characters after that.

code.code:
string word = "Java";
Console.WriteLine(word.Substring(1, 2)); // av
code.caption: Substring(1, 2) starts at index 1 (the second character) and takes 2 characters: "a" and "v".

blocks.question: What does "Java".Substring(1, 2) return?
blocks.explanation: Substring(1, 2) starts at index 1 and takes 2 characters, which are "a" and "v".

blocks.robotComment: Once created, a string's text is locked in for good. 🔒
blocks.body: Strings are immutable: once a string object is created, its contents can never change. Methods like Substring() don't modify the original string — they return a brand-new string with the result. This also means you can safely use == to compare two strings in C#: it checks their actual text content, not just whether they are the same object in memory. The .Equals() method does the same comparison and is often used interchangeably with ==.

code.caption: Because C#'s == is defined to compare content for strings, both lines print True.

blocks.statement: In C#, the == operator compares the actual text content of two strings, not merely whether they are the exact same object.
blocks.explanation: C# specifically overloads == for string so it compares content — unlike the default behavior for most other reference types.

questions.statement: string is a primitive type in C#, just like int or bool.
questions.explanation: string is a reference type — it stores a reference to a string object, not the text directly.

questions.question: What does the + operator do when used with two strings?
questions.explanation: The + operator joins two strings together into one.

questions.sentence: The ___ property returns how many characters are in a string.
questions.explanation: Length is a property (no parentheses) that reports the character count.

questions.question: What does "Java"[0] return?
questions.explanation: Square brackets access a single character by index, and indexing starts at 0.

questions.statement: String indexes, like those used with [] and Substring(), start counting at 0.
questions.explanation: C# strings are zero-indexed, just like arrays.

questions.sentence: "Java".Substring(1, 2) returns ___.
questions.explanation: Substring(1, 2) starts at index 1 and takes 2 characters: "a" and "v".

questions.question: Which is the correct way to compare the text content of two strings in C#?
questions.explanation: C# overloads == for string to compare content, so both == and .Equals() work correctly.

questions.statement: Once created, the contents of a string object can be changed directly.
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable — methods like Substring() return a new string rather than modifying the original.

questions.sentence: Concatenating a string with a number using + automatically ___ the number to text.
questions.explanation: The + operator converts non-string operands to their text representation when combined with a string.

questions.question: What is generally the cleanest way to combine fixed text with a variable value in C#?
questions.explanation: String interpolation ($"...") is usually the cleanest, most readable way to weave values into text.

blocks.robotComment: Some values should just never change — const makes that a promise. 🔒
blocks.body: Sometimes a value should never change once it's set — think of the number of days in a week, or the maximum number of players allowed in a game. C# lets you mark a variable as a compile-time constant using the const keyword, which tells the compiler this value must never change, and must be fully known before the program even runs.

code.code:
const double Pi = 3.14159;
Console.WriteLine(Pi);
code.caption: Declaring a constant with const — Pi can be read, but never reassigned.

blocks.body: A const has to be assigned a value right where it is declared, and that value must be something the compiler can work out immediately — a fixed number, string, or simple expression. You can't use const for something that is only known once the program is running, such as the current time or a value typed in by a user.

highlights.text: assigned a value right where it is declared

blocks.sentence: The ___ keyword marks a variable as a value that must be known at compile time and can never change.
blocks.explanation: const declares a compile-time constant: its value must be fixed and known before the program runs.

blocks.robotComment: readonly is const's more flexible cousin. 🧩
blocks.body: For a value that must never change but is only known once the program starts running — such as a timestamp — C# offers a second keyword: readonly. A readonly field can be assigned once, either where it is declared or inside the class's constructor (which you will meet soon), and after that its value is locked in for good. Unlike const, readonly can only be used on fields that belong to a class, not on local variables inside a method.

code.caption: StartedAt is fixed once the program starts, even though DateTime.Now could never be known at compile time.

blocks.robotComment: This one small capitalization choice sets C# apart from a lot of other languages. 🔠
blocks.body: By convention, constant names in C# are written in PascalCase — every word capitalized, with no underscores, such as MaxPlayers or DaysInWeek. This matches the same PascalCase style used for class names, and instantly marks a name as a constant or fixed value to anyone reading the code.

code.code:
const int MaxPlayers = 4;
Console.WriteLine(MaxPlayers);
code.caption: MaxPlayers follows the PascalCase convention that C# developers use for constants.

blocks.question: What is the key difference between const and readonly in C#?
options: const must be known at compile time; readonly can be assigned once at runtime
const can be changed later; readonly can never be changed
readonly only works with numbers; const works with any type
There is no real difference between them
blocks.explanation: const values must be fully known before the program runs, while readonly values can be computed once when the program starts, then locked in.

blocks.statement: A const field can be assigned a value that is only known while the program is running, such as DateTime.Now.
blocks.explanation: const requires a value the compiler can determine ahead of time. A runtime-only value like DateTime.Now must instead use readonly.

blocks.robotComment: Converting between types isn't always free — some directions are riskier. 🔄
blocks.body: Type casting means converting a value from one type to another. C# has two kinds: implicit (widening) casting, which happens automatically when no data can be lost, and explicit (narrowing) casting, which you must write yourself because it risks losing information.

code.caption: Widening happens automatically because every int value fits perfectly inside a double.

blocks.robotComment: Explicit casts are C#'s way of making you own the risk. ✍️
blocks.body: Going the other way — from a larger or more precise type to a smaller one, like double to int — is called narrowing, and C# requires you to write an explicit cast: the target type in parentheses right before the value. This forces you to acknowledge that some information might be lost.

code.caption: Casting a double to int truncates (cuts off) the decimal part — it does not round.

blocks.robotComment: Overflow bugs are sneaky — the number doesn't error, it just lies. 🐛
blocks.body: Precision loss isn't limited to decimals: casting a whole-number type into a smaller one can also lose data if the value doesn't fit. When that happens, the number can "wrap around" into a completely unexpected — even negative — result, which is a common source of subtle bugs.

code.caption: Casting a value too large to fit into int causes it to overflow instead of simply being cut down.

blocks.sentence: Converting a larger type into a smaller one, such as double to int, is called ___ casting and requires an explicit cast.
blocks.explanation: Narrowing casting risks losing data, so C# requires you to explicitly request it with (targetType).

blocks.question: What does casting the double 9.99 to an int produce?
blocks.explanation: Casting a double to int simply cuts off the decimal part rather than rounding.

blocks.statement: Widening a value, such as converting an int to a double, happens automatically in C#.
blocks.explanation: Widening never loses data, so C# performs it implicitly without requiring a cast.

questions.question: Why are constants useful in code?
options: They replace unexplained "magic numbers" with clearly named, protected values
They make the program run faster than variables
They allow a value to change anywhere in the program
They remove the need for a variable type
questions.explanation: Named constants make code more readable and prevent accidental changes to important fixed values.

questions.explanation: This is implicit widening — every int value fits exactly inside a double.

questions.sentence: Converting a larger type into a smaller one, such as double to int, is called ___ casting.
questions.explanation: Narrowing casting risks losing data, so C# requires an explicit cast.

questions.question: What does casting the double 9.99 to an int produce?
questions.explanation: Casting truncates the decimal part rather than rounding it.

questions.statement: Explicit (narrowing) casting requires you to write the target type in parentheses before the value.
questions.explanation: The syntax (targetType)value is how C# requires an explicit narrowing cast to be written.

questions.sentence: Casting a whole-number value that is too large to fit into a smaller type can cause it to ___.
questions.explanation: A value too large for the target type can wrap around into an unexpected result instead of erroring.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of implicit (widening) casting?
questions.explanation: Assigning an int directly to a double needs no explicit cast, since no precision can be lost.
